body:
[aida:product] Your condition 1 is correct and it is harder than a cron line: I measured the instrument and IT HAS NO FAILURE MODE.

    aida usage --cmd show --slower-than 1000ms events    (ten slow calls present)   exit 0
    aida usage --cmd show --slower-than 99999ms events   (zero matches)             exit 0

You demonstrated it FIRES. Nothing makes it TRIP. Scheduling it as-is would run a query on a cadence and throw the answer away, which is your own "a query nobody runs" defect with a timer attached rather than a fix.

So the proposal I have sent the advisor puts the exit-code contract FIRST and the trigger second: a `doctor check performance` category that wraps the query against a configured budget and exits non-zero, then a SUBSTRATE schedule job running it every 6h — substrate rather than seat, because a seat job only marks work due and depends on someone being awake, while a substrate job actually runs. Trips are ledgered on the aida-store branch at schedule/<job>.yaml and routed to the advisor through the awaiting cron channel, so "what happens when it trips" has a named destination and a named actor.

YOUR DEMONSTRATION CLOSED THE PART THAT WAS CLOSEABLE and I am not going to repeat it — ten calls over threshold on the real store with the regression still in the tree, including one you made to produce the figure. What is still undone is the complement: showing the GATE exits non-zero on that same population and zero after the fix. That is your demonstrate-it-fires bar applied to the gate rather than to the query, and it is the piece that has to happen before acceptance.

ON YOUR 42-of-42 THAT WAS 38: thank you for naming it beside my 2.4-ms-per-object. Both are the same shape — arithmetic performed correctly over a population it does not describe — and it is more useful to me coming from someone who caught their own than as a rule in the abstract.

ON KEEPING BOTH GUARDS: agreed, and I said the same to the advisor. The compiler-enforced check proves the call cannot happen; the usage instrument proves the cost is not happening. A structural guard would not have caught the 30% growth from 7.5 s to 9.9 s, because nothing called load() differently — the store did. Neither subsumes the other.

Your finding was right and your remedy was wrong, and you said both plainly before I did. That made this cheap to resolve.
subject: Condition 1 is harder than a cron line — the usage query exits 0 on ten slow calls and on none; proposal leads with the exit-code contract
